findings.finding: The plan says rebar's write path 'already rides out ref-lock conflicts with retries' and uses that as the safety net for a `<ref>.lock` left by a killed `git reflog expire`. The code does not support this for a lock that is never released. `_with_index_lock_retry` retries git lock errors about 10 times over about 21 s. Only `index.lock` is ever reclaimed. Ref, HEAD and packed-refs locks are 'purely ridden out' on the stated assumption that git holds them 'for microseconds'. So if the expiry is SIGKILLed after the 5 s grace and leaves its lock behind, every later commit uses up the retry budget and fails, and nothing clears the lock until an operator removes it.

scenarios: The expiry ignores SIGTERM for the 5 s grace and is SIGKILLed. A `refs/heads/<branch>.lock` or worktree `HEAD.lock` stays behind, and every later ticket write fails after about 21 s of retries with 'git lock still contended'.

findings.finding: The 124 warning relies on a false premise: "rebar's write path already rides out ref-lock conflicts with retries". findings.finding: The timed-out (124) reflog-expiry arm says a killed expiry 'may leave a `<ref>.lock` behind' and that 'rebar's write path already rides out ref-lock conflicts with retries'. With 3 refs (`--all`), the expiry locks refs/remotes/origin/<branch> as well as HEAD and refs/heads/<branch>.
findings.finding: `git reflog expire --all` runs unconditionally after every write. It takes the ref lock of every ref that has a reflog, including the remote-tracking ref, while rebar's fetches update those refs outside the write lock. A collision makes the fetch fail outright, because a held lock file is not a retried CAS mismatch. The plan gives no reason to run expiry on every write rather than on a cadence.

ABSENCE: the runbook gives no command shape that ties the repack child's lifetime to the lock holder, such as `run_git_reaped` or a process group killed in the `finally`, and gives no instruction for an interrupted session.
findings.finding: The runbook says to hold `rebar._store.lock.write_lock` while running a roughly 605 s full repack from an operator session inside the container. It never says how the repack child is bound to that lock: run as a reaped or process-group child of the lock holder, or killed if the holder dies. The write lock's kernel leg is released when the holder process dies. So if the SSM or `docker exec` session drops, or the Python holder is interrupted, writers can take the lock back while `repack -a -d --cruft` is still running. The reclaim then races live writes, which is the orphaned-git-outside-the-write-lock failure that bug nickelic-lazuline-gonolek fixed.

findings.finding: The runbook says the cruft reclaim needs no rollback because 'only unreachable objects older than 2 weeks are removed'. But unreachable ticket commits are exactly what `rebar store fsck-recover` recovers: it scans `git fsck --no-reflogs` for `dangling commit` lines matching the ticket-commit pattern and cherry-picks them. The reclaim therefore permanently deletes the recovery input for any stranded ticket write older than 2 weeks. It is a one-way deletion with no pre-check for dangling ticket commits and no backup or back-out step.
findings.location: Approach §2 `infra/runbooks/tickets-store-prune.md` — 'Verify by re-measuring. No rollback is needed: only unreachable objects older than 2 weeks are removed.'
scenarios: A write was stranded by a rebase/merge more than 2 weeks ago, and nobody ran fsck-recover. The operator runs the reclaim, the dangling ticket commit's objects go into the expired set and are deleted, and a later fsck-recover finds 'No dangling ticket commits found'. The ticket event is permanently lost.
An abandoned merge left ticket commits that were never re-applied. The reclaim deletes them with no way to restore.
findings.suggested_fix: In tickets-store-prune.md, add a pre-reclaim step: run `git fsck --no-reflogs`, keep the `dangling commit` SHAs whose subject matches the ticket-commit pattern, and stop if any exist until `rebar store fsck-recover` has re-applied them or they are saved (e.g. `git bundle create /backup/dangling-<date>.bundle <shas>` or tag them under `refs/rescue/`). Also copy `.git/objects/pack` aside before the repack, and delete that copy only after the re-measure passes. Rewrite 'No rollback is needed' to describe the backup as the back-out.

findings.finding: The runbook claims the cruft repack 'drops unreachable objects older than 2 weeks from packs'. For objects stored in packs, git judges age by the pack's mtime, not the object's. The store's own write-locked step runs `loose-objects` (packing unreachable loose objects into fresh `loose-*` packs) and `incremental-repack` (rewriting small packs into new ones). Unreachable objects therefore keep receiving fresh pack mtimes and may never look 2 weeks old. The reclaim could remove few or none of the measured ≤157 objects, so the decision's operator-reclaim leg may not deliver.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Correct the worst-case lock-hold statement to include `run_git_reaped`'s reap overhead (5 s SIGTERM grace + 5 s drain per timed-out call, gitutil.py:210/241). That gives about maintenance bound + 30 s + up to 10 s per call, not 'maintenance bound plus 30 s'.
evidence: src/rebar/_store/gitutil.py:210 "_REAP_GRACE_S = 5.0"
src/rebar/_store/gitutil.py:241 "reap_process_group(proc, grace=_REAP_GRACE_S, drain=5.0, label=\"git\", logger=logger)"
findings.finding: The plan says that with a fixed 30 s timeout 'the worst-case lock hold is the maintenance bound plus 30 s'. That ignores how `run_git_reaped` behaves on timeout. The process group is reaped with a 5 s SIGTERM grace and a 5 s drain (`reap_process_group(proc, grace=_REAP_GRACE_S, drain=5.0)`). So each reaped call can run up to about 10 s past its timeout, and the worst case with both calls is about the maintenance bound + 30 s + 20 s.
findings.location: Approach §1, first bullet ("so the worst-case lock hold is the maintenance bound plus 30 s")
scenarios: Maintenance runs to just under 120 s, then the expiry hangs. The write lock is held for about 120 + 30 + 10 s, while writers wait at most 30 s x 2. This limit is now understated in both the plan and the updated docs.
findings.suggested_fix: Reword it as: 'worst-case lock hold ≈ maintenance timeout + 30 s expiry timeout, each plus up to 10 s of reap grace/drain'.

evidence: Plan measures only `--dry-run`. Without --dry-run, git writes each kept entry to a `logs/<ref>.lock` file and commits it, so a ~4.7 MB file is rewritten even when nothing has expired (the clone is younger than 90 days, so almost nothing expires today).
The step runs under the write lock after every commit (event_append.py:99, txn.py:120), so its cost is added to every write's lock hold.
findings.finding: The cost evidence is a `--dry-run`, which skips the work the real command does on every write: locking each ref and its log, then rewriting the whole reflog file (HEAD is 4.69 MB / 25,933 entries) and renaming it into place. The plan says nothing about the per-write lock-hold and latency cost of the real expiry.

scenarios: A slow or fsync-heavy EBS volume makes the per-write rewrite of ~5 MB of reflogs noticeably longer than the dry-run figure, and that time is added to every ticket write's lock hold.

git-gc(1) (man.archlinux.org, retrieved): 'When git gc is run, it will call prune --expire 2.weeks.ago (and repack --cruft --cruft-expiration 2.weeks.ago if using cruft packs ...)'. Stock gc pairs the cruft repack with a prune and does not rely on the repack alone.

findings.finding: The runbook asserts that `git -c pack.threads=1 repack -a -d --cruft --cruft-expiration=2.weeks.ago` 'drops unreachable objects older than 2 weeks from packs and loose storage', but nothing backs this up. git's documented gc flow runs `git prune --expire` IN ADDITION TO the cruft repack. `repack -d` only runs `prune-packed`, which deletes loose files already present in a pack. An expired unreachable loose object is left out of the cruft pack, so it is not in any pack and likely stays on disk as a loose file.

findings.finding: The runbook's reclaim command `git -c pack.threads=1 repack -a -d --cruft --cruft-expiration=2.weeks.ago` is described as dropping "unreachable objects older than 2 weeks from packs and loose storage". As far as I know it only removes PACKED copies. Expired unreachable LOOSE objects are left out of the cruft pack, and repack's loose-object cleanup (prune-packed) only deletes loose objects that are now in a pack, so those loose objects stay on disk. git gc itself runs `git prune --expire` after a cruft repack for this reason. The plan also never checked the `--cruft` / `--cruft-expiration` flags against git 2.47.3, although it did check `maintenance` against that version.
